entries.lesson_core_move: Map each time feature in x(t) to t0/a in x(at) for a>1 and identify the resulting waveform as compressed toward t=0 with unchanged amplitudes.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Time Compression
sections.learning_goal: Explain that $y(t)=x(at)$ with $a>1$ compresses every time feature toward $t=0$ by the factor $1/a$ while leaving amplitudes unchanged.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image required; the step is fully symbolic.

question_policy.answer_format: not applicable
question_policy.practice_question_model: No practice questions are generated for the tutorial step.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Teach the time-scaling rule for $y(t)=x(at)$ when $a>1$: replace each time feature at $t_0$ with $t_0/a$ and read the result as a compression toward $t=0$ with unchanged amplitudes.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Start with $y(t)=x(2t)$ and show that a feature at $t_0$ in $x(t)$ appears at $t_0/2$ in $y(t)$.
paragraph_plan: State the transform $y(t)=x(at)$ and the rule for the case $a>1$.
Use the base case $y(t)=x(2t)$ to anchor the idea that larger input times appear earlier.
Generalize from the base case to any $a>1$ and conclude that every time feature moves to $t_0/a$.
Close by emphasizing that only horizontal spacing changes and amplitudes stay the same.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Not applicable; this is the tutorial step.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the rule in the first paragraph and avoid introducing time reversal, time shift, or amplitude scaling.

sections.section_title: Recognizing x(at) as Time Compression for a>1
sections.learning_goal: Recognize $x(at)$ with $a>1$ as a time-compressed version of $x(t)$ and name the direction of the change.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image required; the recognition task is purely symbolic.

question_policy.answer_format: Five answer choices with one correct symbolic classification.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Given $y(t)=x(5t)$, choose the correct description of the transform and whether the feature times move closer to or farther from $t=0$.
distractor_plan: Use expansion instead of compression.
Confuse time scaling with a time shift.
Confuse time scaling with amplitude scaling.
Confuse $a>1$ with time reversal.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Set up the recognition rule: when $a>1$, the factor inside $x(at)$ makes time run faster, so the output is compressed toward $t=0$.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Use $y(t)=x(2t)$ to show that doubling the input time halves every feature location.
paragraph_plan: State the recognition question: what horizontal change does $x(at)$ produce when $a>1$?
Use the base case $x(2t)$ to anchor the idea that larger input times appear earlier.
Generalize to any $a>1$ and conclude that the waveform is compressed toward $t=0$.
Remind the reader that vertical amplitudes are unchanged.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Given $y(t)=x(4t)$, determine whether the signal is compressed or expanded and state what happens to the feature at $t_0=6$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that the factor $4$ compresses the signal by $1/4$ and that the feature at $t=6$ moves to $t=6/4$.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Compared with the tutorial rule, this asks the learner to identify the transform from the factor alone and apply it to one named feature.
solution_step_plan: Read the factor inside the argument and note that $4>1$.
Classify the waveform as compressed toward $t=0$.
Map the marked feature at $t_0=6$ to $t_0/4$.
State that the amplitude of the feature does not change.
practice_variation_axes: Use different compression factors such as $2$, $3$, or $5$.
Vary the named time feature location.
Ask for the classification only or the feature location plus classification.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the worked example purely symbolic and make the wrong answers target expansion, shift, reversal, and amplitude-scaling confusion.

sections.section_title: Mapping a Single Time Feature Under Compression
sections.learning_goal: Map one marked time feature from $t_0$ in $x(t)$ to $t_0/a$ in $x(at)$.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image required; one feature can be tracked directly from notation.

question_policy.answer_format: Five answer choices with one correct mapped time location.
question_policy.practice_question_model: If $x(t)$ has a peak at $t=8$, where does that peak appear in $y(t)=x(4t)$?
distractor_plan: Multiply the time by the factor instead of dividing.
Leave the feature at the original time.
Move the feature by a constant shift.
Treat the transform as a reversal instead of a compression.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Show how to compute the new location of one feature by solving $at=t_0$ for $t$.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Use a peak at $t_0=6$ under $y(t)=x(3t)$ so the location is easy to compute.
paragraph_plan: Name the feature in $x(t)$ and write the matching equation $at=t_0$.
Solve for the new time $t=t_0/a$.
Check the answer with the base case $t_0=6$ and $a=3$.
Reinforce that the feature value stays the same while only its time changes.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: If $x(t)$ has a peak at $t=6$, where does that peak appear in $y(t)=x(3t)$?
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Solve $3t=6$ to locate the peak at $t=2$ and state that the peak height is unchanged.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This example moves from classification to exact feature mapping for a single marked point.
solution_step_plan: Set the input-time feature equation $3t=6$.
Solve for the new time $t=2$.
State the mapped feature location in $y(t)$.
Confirm that the peak amplitude is unchanged.
practice_variation_axes: Change the original feature time.
Change the compression factor.
Use a valley, zero-crossing, or labeled corner instead of a peak.
Ask for the mapped time only or the mapped time plus unchanged amplitude.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the algebra minimal and force the learner to map the time coordinate directly.

sections.section_title: Compressing Support Intervals and Durations
sections.learning_goal: Compress an interval of nonzero support by mapping both endpoints to their divided-by-$a$ locations.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image required; the support interval can be tracked symbolically.

question_policy.answer_format: Five answer choices with one correct support interval.
question_policy.practice_question_model: If $x(t)$ is nonzero on $[3,9]$, what is the support of $y(t)=x(3t)$ and how does its duration change?
distractor_plan: Multiply the endpoints by $a$ instead of dividing by $a$.
Leave the interval unchanged.
Reverse the interval order.
Apply a shift instead of a scaling.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Show that if $x(t)$ is nonzero on an interval, then $x(at)$ is nonzero on the same interval shrunk by $1/a$.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Use a simple support like $[2,10]$ under $y(t)=x(2t)$.
paragraph_plan: Identify the support interval in $x(t)$.
Map each endpoint through $t=t_0/a$.
Compute the new interval length and compare it to the original.
Conclude that the whole support is squeezed toward $t=0$ with the same amplitudes.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: If $x(t)$ is nonzero on $[2,10]$, what is the support of $y(t)=x(2t)$?
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Map both endpoints to $1$ and $5$ and state that the support length is halved.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This example extends single-feature mapping to the entire active interval, including both endpoints.
solution_step_plan: Identify the original support endpoints $2$ and $10$.
Divide each endpoint by $2$.
Write the new support interval $[1,5]$.
State that the duration shrinks from $8$ to $4$ while amplitudes stay unchanged.
practice_variation_axes: Change the support endpoints.
Change the compression factor.
Use an interval stated with open or closed endpoints.
Ask for the new support and the new duration.

sections.handoff_notes: Make endpoint mapping explicit so the writer does not drift into a generic duration-change explanation.

sections.section_title: Reading a Compressed Waveform with Unchanged Amplitudes
sections.learning_goal: Interpret the full compressed waveform by combining feature locations, support, and unchanged heights.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image required; the final interpretation is a symbolic summary of the earlier rules.

question_policy.answer_format: Five answer choices with one correct full-waveform description.
question_policy.practice_question_model: A waveform with a peak at $t=6$ and support $[2,14]$ is transformed to $y(t)=x(2t)$. Describe the new peak time, support, and amplitude behavior.
distractor_plan: Change the amplitudes instead of leaving them unchanged.
Describe a time shift instead of a compression.
Describe a reversal instead of a compression.
Expand the time axis instead of compressing it.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Show how to read a completed compressed waveform by checking feature locations and support first, then confirming that amplitudes are unchanged.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Use a waveform with one peak at $t=4$ and support on $[1,7]$ under $y(t)=x(2t)$.
paragraph_plan: Summarize the earlier rules: each time feature moves to $t_0/a$ and amplitudes stay the same.
Read the compressed waveform by checking a single peak and the support interval together.
Use the base case to show the entire shape is squeezed toward $t=0$.
Finish by restating the combined description in one sentence.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: A waveform $x(t)$ has a peak at $t=4$ and is nonzero on $[1,7]$. Describe the waveform $y(t)=x(2t)$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Read the whole compressed waveform as having the peak at $t=2$, support $[1/2,7/2]$, and the same peak height as $x(t)$.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This example combines a feature location and a support interval so the learner must read the full waveform, not just one coordinate.
solution_step_plan: Map the peak time $4$ to $4/2=2$.
Map the support endpoints $1$ and $7$ to $1/2$ and $7/2$.
State the compressed waveform description in one sentence.
Explicitly note that the amplitudes are unchanged.
practice_variation_axes: Change the peak location and support interval.
Change the compression factor.
Add an additional feature such as a zero crossing or second peak.
Ask for a full verbal description of the compressed waveform.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the final description compact and emphasize that only the horizontal geometry changed.

entries.lesson_core_move: Map each time feature in x(t) to t0/a in x(at) for 0<a<1 and identify the resulting waveform as expanded away from t=0 with unchanged amplitudes.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Time Expansion
sections.learning_goal: Teach the learner that replacing $t$ by $at$ with $0<a<1$ expands a signal away from $t=0$ without changing amplitudes.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the rule is clearer when stated symbolically.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate an image for this step.

question_policy.answer_format: not-applicable
question_policy.practice_question_model: No practice questions for the tutorial step.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Establish the general scaling rule $y(t)=x(at)$ and the special case $0<a<1$ as time expansion.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Use $x(t/2)$ as the clean base case so one labeled feature moves from $t_0$ to $2t_0$ while its height stays the same.
paragraph_plan: State the general rule $y(t)=x(at)$ and mark $0<a<1$ as the expansion case.
Use $x(t/2)$ to show how one labeled feature moves from $t_0$ to $2t_0$.
Explain that every other time feature follows the same $t_0/a$ rule, so the whole waveform stretches away from $t=0$.
Close by emphasizing that the amplitudes do not change; only the time locations change.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Not applicable for the tutorial step.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Not applicable for the tutorial step.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Not applicable for the tutorial step.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the opening compact, then move immediately to the first concrete scaling case before any practice appears.

sections.section_title: Recognizing x(t/2) as a Time Expansion
sections.learning_goal: Recognize $x(t/2)$ as a time expansion and identify the stretch factor as $2$.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the classification can be done directly from the symbolic form.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate an image for this step.

question_policy.answer_format: Symbolic multiple-choice with one correct expansion classification.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Which transformed signal is a time expansion of $x(t)$ by factor $3$?
distractor_plan: Compression choice such as $x(3t)$ instead of the expansion.
No-change choice such as $x(t)$.
Amplitude-change choice such as $2x(t)$.
Shift or reversal distractor such as $x(t-3)$ or $x(-t)$.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Not applicable for this example step.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Not applicable for this example step.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Decide whether $x(t/2)$ is a time expansion or a time compression, and state the stretch factor.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that $x(t/2)$ means $a=1/2$, so every time feature moves to twice its original time and the signal is expanded by factor $2$.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Moves from the rule statement to classifying one specific transformed signal.
solution_step_plan: Identify $a=1/2$ from the expression $x(t/2)$.
Check one landmark time and confirm it becomes $2t_0$.
State that all landmark times follow the same doubling rule.
Conclude that the waveform is expanded away from $t=0$ with unchanged amplitudes.
practice_variation_axes: Use other fractional scale factors such as $1/3$ or $1/4$.
Ask for the expansion factor or the classification.
Vary the wording of the signal expression while keeping the same $x(at)$ structure.

sections.handoff_notes: Stay on the recognition step: the later questions should test whether the learner can name the expansion factor from a single transformed expression.

sections.section_title: Mapping Original Time Points to t0/a
sections.learning_goal: Map each original time point $t_0$ to the new location $t_0/a$ in $x(at)$ when $0<a<1$.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the learner can map landmark times from the symbolic rule alone.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate an image for this step.

question_policy.answer_format: Symbolic/numeric multiple-choice with one correct mapped time.
question_policy.practice_question_model: If a feature occurs at $t_0=-6$ and the signal becomes $x(t/3)$, where does that feature move?
distractor_plan: Multiply the time by the factor instead of dividing by it.
Keep the time unchanged.
Drop or flip the sign of the original time.
Confuse the expansion with a shift.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Not applicable for this example step.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Not applicable for this example step.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: A feature is located at $t_0=-6$ in $x(t)$. If the signal becomes $x(t/3)$, where does that feature move, and what is the general rule for any $t_0$?
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that $a=1/3$ sends the feature to $t_0/a=-18$ and generalize the rule to $t_0/a$ for every landmark time.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Adds explicit landmark mapping instead of only naming the transformed signal.
solution_step_plan: Read the scale factor as $a=1/3$.
Apply the mapping $t_0 \mapsto t_0/a$ to the given feature time.

Change the scale factor while keeping $0<a<1$.
Ask for the mapped time directly or for the general mapping rule.

sections.section_title: Finding Expanded Support with Unchanged Amplitude
sections.learning_goal: Determine the new support interval of $x(at)$ and keep the amplitudes unchanged.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; support endpoints and amplitudes can be handled symbolically.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate an image for this step.

distractor_plan: Multiply the support endpoints by $a$ instead of dividing them.
Keep the support interval unchanged.
Shift the interval instead of stretching it.
Claim the amplitude scales with the time stretch.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Not applicable for this example step.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Not applicable for this example step.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: If $x(t)$ is nonzero on $[1,3]$ and has peak amplitude $5$, find the support of $x(t/2)$ and state what happens to the amplitude.

example_outline.variation_from_previous: Extends point mapping to an entire support interval and checks that amplitudes do not change.
solution_step_plan: Map the left and right support endpoints through $t_0/a$ with $a=1/2$.
Write the new support interval as $[2,6]$.

Pair the interval question with an explicit amplitude-preservation check.

entries.lesson_core_move: Convert a piecewise signal x(t) into x(at) for a>0 by mapping each breakpoint t0 to t0/a and replacing t with at in the formula assigned to each scaled interval.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Time Scaling of Piecewise Signals
sections.learning_goal: Explain that $x(at)$ keeps each piece's values intact while moving every breakpoint to $t_0/a$ and rewriting each interval formula with $at$.

question_policy.answer_format: No questions in this tutorial section.
question_policy.practice_question_model: No practice questions; this section is direct instruction only.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Teach the one-rule transformation for a piecewise definition under $x(at)$: solve $at=t_0$ for each breakpoint and substitute $at$ into each interval formula.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Use a two-piece signal with one breakpoint and constant values so the learner sees the breakpoint move before any formula algebra.
paragraph_plan: State that time scaling changes when the pieces occur, not the values assigned to them.
Show the breakpoint rule by solving $at=t_0$, which places the new breakpoint at $t_0/a$.
Walk through a simple two-piece signal so the learner sees the new interval boundary in context.
Show how each interval formula is rewritten by replacing $t$ with $at$.
Close by checking the final piecewise definition and noting that $a>1$ compresses while $0<a<1$ expands.
display_math_plan: $$x(t)=\begin{cases}f_1(t), & t_0\le t<t_1\\f_2(t), & t_1\le t<t_2\end{cases} \Rightarrow x(at)=\begin{cases}f_1(at), & t_0/a\le t<t_1/a\\f_2(at), & t_1/a\le t<t_2/a\end{cases}$$

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the section symbolic and minimal; the later examples should carry the worked-example load.

sections.section_title: Scaling the Breakpoints of a Simple Piecewise Signal
sections.learning_goal: Move the breakpoint of a two-piece constant signal under $x(at)$ and keep the piece values unchanged.

question_policy.answer_format: Five symbolic piecewise-definition choices; one correct answer.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Ask for the correct piecewise definition of $x(at)$ for a two-piece constant signal with one breakpoint; vary the breakpoint and the scale factor while keeping the formulas constant.
distractor_plan: Leave the breakpoint unchanged.
Multiply the breakpoint by $a$ instead of dividing by $a$.
Swap the left and right piece values.
Change the constant values even though only time is being scaled.
Use the correct values but attach them to the wrong side of the breakpoint.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Find $x(3t)$ for $$x(t)=\begin{cases}2,& t<6\\-1,& t\ge 6\end{cases}$$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that the breakpoint moves from $6$ to $2$ and that the constant values stay the same on the new intervals.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Compared with the tutorial, this example isolates breakpoint movement by using constants so no formula algebra is needed.
solution_step_plan: Identify the scale factor $a=3$ and solve $3t=6$ for the new breakpoint.
Divide the original breakpoint by $3$ to get $2$.
Keep the constant values $2$ and $-1$ attached to the corresponding intervals.
Write the transformed piecewise definition and verify the interval order.
practice_variation_axes: Change the original breakpoint.
Change the scale factor $a>1$.
Use different constant values on the two pieces.
Place the breakpoint at a non-multiple of $a$.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the worked example short and algebra-free; the learner should only be dividing the breakpoint and preserving constant amplitudes.

sections.section_title: Rewriting Piecewise Formulas After Replacing t with at
sections.learning_goal: Rewrite each interval formula after substituting $at$ and relocate the breakpoint at the same time.

question_policy.answer_format: Five symbolic piecewise-definition choices; one correct answer.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Ask for the correct piecewise definition of $x(at)$ when the original signal has two nonconstant intervals; vary the slopes and intercepts so the learner must substitute $at$ into each formula.
distractor_plan: Move the breakpoint correctly but forget to replace $t$ inside one formula.
Use the original breakpoint instead of dividing it by $a$.
Substitute $t/a$ instead of $at$ into a formula.
Swap the formulas assigned to the two intervals.
Make an arithmetic slip when simplifying the substituted expressions.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Find $x(2t)$ for $$x(t)=\begin{cases}t+1,& 0\le t<2\\3-t,& 2\le t<4\end{cases}$$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show how each formula changes when $t$ is replaced by $2t$ and how the breakpoint $2$ moves to $1$.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Unlike the previous example, the formulas now depend on $t$, so the learner must rewrite the expressions inside each interval as well as the breakpoint.
solution_step_plan: Identify the original intervals and solve $2t=2$ to locate the new breakpoint.
Substitute $2t$ into the first formula and simplify to $2t+1$.
Substitute $2t$ into the second formula and simplify to $3-2t$.
Assemble the new piecewise definition with the transformed intervals.
practice_variation_axes: Change the linear formulas.
Change the number of intervals to three.
Use a different compression factor.
Move the breakpoint away from $0$.
Mix constant and linear pieces.

sections.handoff_notes: Make the substitution step explicit so the learner sees the difference between moving breakpoints and rewriting formulas.

sections.section_title: Time Compression of a Multi-Interval Piecewise Signal
sections.learning_goal: Apply the same breakpoint and substitution rules across several intervals when $a>1$ compresses a multi-interval signal.

question_policy.answer_format: Five symbolic piecewise-definition choices; one correct answer.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Ask for the correct compressed piecewise definition of a multi-interval signal under $x(at)$ with $a>1$; vary the number of breakpoints and include one nonconstant interval so both breakpoint mapping and substitution are required.
distractor_plan: Divide only the first breakpoint and leave the rest unchanged.
Multiply each breakpoint by $a$ instead of dividing by $a$.
Rewrite only part of the interval formulas.
Leave the formulas unchanged even though $t$ was replaced by $at$.
Reverse the piece order after compression.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Find $x(2t)$ for $$x(t)=\begin{cases}0,& t<1\\t-1,& 1\le t<3\\2,& t\ge 3\end{cases}$$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that each breakpoint is divided by $2$ and each interval formula is evaluated at $2t$.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This extends the two-piece example to three intervals so the learner must track more than one breakpoint without changing the underlying rule.
solution_step_plan: List the original breakpoints in order and divide each by $2$.
Rewrite the middle formula by replacing $t$ with $2t$.
Keep the constant pieces unchanged.
Assemble the compressed signal from left to right using the new breakpoints.
practice_variation_axes: Use three or four intervals instead of three.
Change the breakpoint locations.
Mix constant, linear, and simple affine pieces.
Change the compression factor while keeping $a>1$.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the question mirrored to the worked example by changing only one numerical detail at a time.

sections.section_title: Time Expansion of a Multi-Interval Piecewise Signal
sections.learning_goal: Apply the same transformation when $0<a<1$ so the piecewise signal expands away from $t=0$.

question_policy.answer_format: Five symbolic piecewise-definition choices; one correct answer.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Ask for the correct expanded piecewise definition of a multi-interval signal under $x(at)$ with $0<a<1$; vary the outward-moved breakpoints and include one nonconstant interval so the learner must substitute $at$ and stretch the intervals.
distractor_plan: Leave the breakpoints unchanged.
Multiply the breakpoints by $a$ instead of by $1/a$.
Use the compressed interval order instead of the expanded one.
Substitute $t$ instead of $t/2$ inside the formulas.
Move the breakpoint in the wrong direction relative to $t=0$.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Find $x(t/2)$ for $$x(t)=\begin{cases}0,& t<1\\t-1,& 1\le t<3\\2,& t\ge 3\end{cases}$$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that the breakpoints move outward to $2$ and $6$ and that each formula is evaluated at $t/2$.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This uses the same original piecewise signal as the compression example, but with $0<a<1$ so the breakpoints move farther from the origin instead of closer.
solution_step_plan: Identify the scale factor $a=1/2$ and solve $(1/2)t=t_0$ for each breakpoint.
Multiply each original breakpoint by $2$ to get the expanded interval boundaries.
Replace $t$ with $t/2$ inside each interval formula.
Write the expanded piecewise definition and check that the ordering still matches the original piece values.
practice_variation_axes: Use a different $0<a<1$ scale factor.
Change the number of intervals.
Change the outer constant pieces.
Use breakpoints that expand to non-integer values.

sections.handoff_notes: Make the expansion explicit in the interval endpoints; this example should look like the compression case with every breakpoint pushed farther from zero.

entries.lesson_core_move: Convert time-scaled exponentials by rewriting e^{s(at)} as e^{(as)t} and interpreting a as changing the growth, decay, or oscillation rate in continuous time.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Time Scaling of Exponentials
sections.learning_goal: Build the rule that time scaling inside the exponent multiplies the exponent coefficient and changes the rate without changing the exponential family.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the step is fully symbolic.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate an image; the tutorial is a symbolic rate-rewrite.

question_policy.answer_format: not-applicable
question_policy.practice_question_model: not-applicable

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Teach the general identity $e^{s(at)} = e^{(as)t}$ and the meaning of $a$ as a rate multiplier for exponential growth, decay, and oscillation.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Start with $e^{-t}$ and show that replacing $t$ by $2t$ gives $e^{-2t}$, which is the same exponential shape compressed toward $t=0$.
paragraph_plan: State the core rule with one short sentence and the display equation $e^{s(at)} = e^{(as)t}$.
Show the algebra on a real exponential first so the learner sees that the factor $a$ multiplies the exponent coefficient.
Explain the interpretation: $a>1$ makes the exponential evolve faster, while $0<a<1$ makes it evolve more slowly.
Add the complex-exponential bridge: the same multiplier changes oscillation rate when the exponent has an imaginary part.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the tutorial short and direct: establish the coefficient-multiplication rule first, then preview that the same rule will govern decay rate and oscillation rate in the examples.

sections.section_title: Rewriting a Time-Scaled Real Exponential
sections.learning_goal: Rewrite a scaled real exponential in standard form and decide whether the decay rate increased or decreased.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the example is an algebraic rewrite of a real exponential.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate an image; use symbolic algebra only.

question_policy.answer_format: Five answer choices showing candidate rewritten exponentials or decay interpretations; one correct rewrite and four algebraic or conceptual distractors.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Rewrite a scaled real exponential such as $e^{-k(at)}$ and choose the correct standard form or decay comparison.
distractor_plan: Divide the coefficient by $a$ instead of multiplying it.
Leave the scale factor inside the time variable without rewriting.
Reverse the faster/slower interpretation for $a>1$ and $0<a<1$.
Change the amplitude rather than the exponent rate.
Keep the exponent coefficient fixed at the unscaled value.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Rewrite $x(t)=e^{-3(2t)}$ in standard form and state how its decay compares with $e^{-3t}$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Reach $x(t)=e^{-6t}$ and conclude that the decay is twice as fast because the exponent coefficient doubled.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This adds concrete numbers to the abstract rule and asks the learner to connect the rewrite to a faster decay rate.
solution_step_plan: Identify the base exponent coefficient $-3$ and the scale factor $a=2$.
Multiply the coefficient by $a$ to get $-6$ and rewrite the signal as $e^{-6t}$.
Compare the effective coefficient with the unscaled case $e^{-3t}$.
State the interpretation: the waveform is compressed toward $t=0$ and decays faster.
practice_variation_axes: Change the real coefficient while keeping the scale factor positive.
Switch between $a>1$ and $0<a<1$.
Ask for either the rewritten form or the faster/slower decay interpretation.
Vary the sign of the exponent so the same rule applies to growth as well as decay.

sections.handoff_notes: Make the worked example a clean coefficient-multiplication exercise, then let the practice questions probe equivalent rewrites and decay-speed comparisons.

sections.section_title: Interpreting Faster and Slower Exponential Decay
sections.learning_goal: Compare scaled decays and use the exponent coefficient to rank signals from fastest to slowest decay.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the comparison is entirely symbolic.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate an image; the skill is comparing effective decay rates algebraically.

question_policy.answer_format: Five answer choices showing candidate decay orders, rewritten exponentials, or rate descriptions; one correct comparison and four plausible distractors.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Given several scaled real decays, choose the signal that decays fastest or the correct ordering by decay rate.
distractor_plan: Order by the raw scale factor instead of the effective exponent coefficient.
Confuse $a>1$ with slower decay.
Treat the unscaled signal as the fastest or slowest by default.
Use the reciprocal scale factor.
Ignore the sign of the exponent coefficient.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Compare $x_1(t)=e^{-2(3t)}$ and $x_2(t)=e^{-2(0.5t)}$ with the unscaled signal $e^{-2t}$; rewrite each and decide which decays fastest, which is unchanged, and which decays slowest.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Rewrite each signal as $e^{-6t}$, $e^{-2t}$, and $e^{-t}$, then order them by decay speed using the size of the effective exponent coefficient.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This shifts from rewriting one signal to comparing several scaled versions so the learner has to interpret relative decay rates.
solution_step_plan: Compute each effective coefficient by multiplying the base rate by the scale factor.
Rewrite the three signals in standard exponential form.
Compare the magnitude of the negative coefficients to order the decay speeds.
Label the compressed case as faster decay and the expanded case as slower decay.
practice_variation_axes: Use different base decay constants.
Mix one compressed case with one expanded case in the same prompt.
Ask for an ordering, a faster/slower label, or an equivalence rewrite.
Include a growth case to check that the same multiplication rule still applies.

sections.handoff_notes: Center the example on rate comparison, not just algebra, so later practice can ask for fastest, slowest, or unchanged decay from the same rewrite rule.

sections.section_title: Scaling the Oscillation Rate of a Complex Exponential
sections.learning_goal: Rewrite a scaled complex exponential and identify the new angular frequency as $a\omega$.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the example is an algebraic rewrite of a complex exponential.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate an image; the step is about frequency scaling in notation.

question_policy.answer_format: Five answer choices showing candidate rewritten complex exponentials or angular-frequency interpretations; one correct rewrite and four distractors.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Rewrite a scaled complex exponential such as $e^{j\omega(at)}$ and choose the correct new angular frequency or equivalent expression.
distractor_plan: Multiply the amplitude instead of the frequency.
Divide the frequency by $a$.
Leave the oscillation rate unchanged.
Drop the imaginary unit and treat the signal as real.
Swap the sign of the frequency without justification.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Rewrite $x(t)=e^{j4(2t)}$ in standard form and state how the oscillation rate compares with $e^{j4t}$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that $x(t)=e^{j8t}$ and conclude that the oscillation rate doubles while amplitude stays unchanged.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This extends the same rewrite rule from decay rates to oscillation rates by moving from a real exponent to an imaginary one.
solution_step_plan: Identify the frequency coefficient $4$ and the time-scaling factor $2$.
Multiply them to get the new angular frequency $8$.
Rewrite the signal as $e^{j8t}$.
Interpret the result as the same amplitude with faster oscillation.
practice_variation_axes: Vary the original angular frequency.
Switch between compression and expansion with $a>1$ and $0<a<1$.
Ask for either the rewritten exponential or the new oscillation rate.
Keep the amplitude implicit so the learner focuses on the exponent.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the worked example frequency-focused: the same multiplier rule now changes oscillation speed rather than decay rate.

sections.section_title: Scaling Both the Envelope and Oscillation of a Damped Sinusoid
sections.learning_goal: Apply the scaling rule to a damped sinusoid so both the envelope and oscillation are tracked together.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the example is an algebraic rewrite of a damped sinusoid.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate an image; the rewrite is fully symbolic.

question_policy.answer_format: Five answer choices showing candidate rewritten damped sinusoids or paired envelope-and-oscillation interpretations; one correct rewrite and four distractors.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Choose the correct standard form and interpretation for a time-scaled damped sinusoid.
distractor_plan: Scale only the real part of the exponent.
Scale only the imaginary part of the exponent.
Swap the real and imaginary parts.
Use the inverse scale factor instead of multiplying.
Misread the result so only one of the envelope or oscillation changes.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Rewrite $x(t)=e^{(-1+j4)(2t)}$ in standard form and identify how both the envelope and oscillation compare with $e^{(-1+j4)t}$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that $x(t)=e^{(-2+j8)t}$, so the envelope decays twice as fast and the oscillation rate doubles.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This final example combines the real and imaginary parts of the exponent so the learner must scale both effects at once.
solution_step_plan: Distribute the scale factor $2$ across both parts of the complex exponent.
Rewrite the signal as $e^{(-2+j8)t}$.
Separate the envelope change from the oscillation change.
State the final interpretation: faster decay and faster oscillation with the same initial amplitude.
practice_variation_axes: Change both the damping and oscillation coefficients.
Use $a>1$ and $0<a<1$ in the same lesson.
Ask for either the full rewritten form or the paired interpretation.
Vary whether the signal is a damped exponential or a damped sinusoid in real form.

sections.handoff_notes: End with the combined case so the learner has to apply the same multiplication rule to both the envelope and the oscillation in one pass.

entries.lesson_title: Comparing Time Shifts and Time Scaling
entries.lesson_core_move: Distinguish time shifts from time scaling by mapping transformed arguments to key-time locations and deciding whether features translate by a constant offset or compress/expand relative to t=0.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Comparing Time Shifts and Time Scaling
sections.learning_goal: Teach the additive-vs-multiplicative rule for a transformed time argument so the learner can tell a shift from a scale by tracking one labeled landmark.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the comparison is fully symbolic and uses labeled times only.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate an image. Keep the step symbolic-only and use text formulas instead of plots.

question_policy.answer_format: No questions in the tutorial section.
question_policy.practice_question_model: N/A

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: State the comparison rule: a shift adds the same offset to every key time, while a scale divides every key time by the scale factor and changes spacing relative to $t=0$.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Use one labeled landmark, such as a peak at $t=3$, and compare its location in $x(t-t_s)$ and $x(at)$.
paragraph_plan: Introduce the reference signal and the single landmark that will be tracked through both transformations.
Show the shift rule with $x(t-t_s)$ and the scale rule with $x(at)$, solving each transformed argument for the original landmark time.
Compare the outcomes: a shift preserves spacing and moves by a constant offset, while scaling changes all times by the same factor about $t=0$.
Close with the decision test: same additive offset means a shift; uniform multiplication of times means a scale.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: N/A for the tutorial step.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: N/A for the tutorial step.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: N/A for the tutorial step.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the introduction compact and symbolic. Do not add practice questions here; the examples will carry the active learning.

sections.section_title: Comparing One Key Time Under a Shift and a Scale
sections.learning_goal: Map one labeled time feature through a shift and through a scale and name the correct transformed locations.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the step uses symbolic time labels only.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate an image. Keep the worked example and questions text-only.

question_policy.answer_format: Five text answer choices; each choice gives the transformed landmark locations or the correct shift/scale classification.
question_policy.practice_question_model: A signal $x(t)$ has a peak at $t=t_0$. In $y_1(t)=x(t-a)$ and $y_2(t)=x(bt)$, which pair of peak locations is correct?
distractor_plan: Add the shift amount to the scaled time instead of solving the transformed argument.
Use division for the shift case and addition for the scale case.
Multiply by $b$ instead of dividing by $b$ in the scaled signal.
Reverse the sign of the shift and place the peak on the wrong side of the reference time.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: N/A for the example step.
tutorial_outline.base_case: N/A for the example step.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: A signal $x(t)$ has a peak at $t=3$. Compare the peak location in $y_1(t)=x(t-2)$ and in $y_2(t)=x(4t)$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that the shifted peak moves to $t=5$ by addition, while the scaled peak moves to $t=3/4$ by division.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Extends the tutorial by applying the rule to one concrete landmark in both a shifted signal and a scaled signal.
solution_step_plan: Identify the landmark time $t=3$ in the reference signal.
Apply the shift rule to $y_1(t)=x(t-2)$ and move the peak to $t=5$.
Apply the scale rule to $y_2(t)=x(4t)$ by solving $4t=3$ and getting $t=3/4$.
State the contrast: the shift adds a constant, while the scale divides the landmark time by the factor.
practice_variation_axes: landmark time
shift amount
scale factor
feature type such as peak, zero crossing, or endpoint

sections.handoff_notes: Stay symbolic. The worked example should make the additive-vs-multiplicative contrast explicit before the questions appear.

sections.section_title: Comparing Multiple Key Times Under a Shift and a Scale
sections.learning_goal: Map several key times through both transformations and use the resulting spacing to compare shift and scale.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the step uses symbolic key-time lists only.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate an image. Keep the example and practice in symbolic form.

question_policy.answer_format: Five text answer choices; each choice lists transformed key times for the shift and the scale.
question_policy.practice_question_model: The signal $x(t)$ has key times at $t=2$, $t=4$, and $t=6$. Which answer choice correctly lists the corresponding key times in $x(t-3)$ and $x(2t)$?
distractor_plan: Shift every time in the scaled case by the same amount instead of dividing.
Multiply the shifted times by $2$ instead of adding the offset.
Preserve the original spacing in the scaled signal.
Apply the shift with the wrong sign.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: N/A for the example step.
tutorial_outline.base_case: N/A for the example step.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: The signal $x(t)$ has key times at $t=2$, $t=4$, and $t=6$. Compare the key times in $y_1(t)=x(t-3)$ and in $y_2(t)=x(2t)$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that each key time in $x(t)$ shifts by the same additive offset in $x(t-3)$ but is divided by $2$ in $x(2t)$, so spacing stays the same only in the shift case.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Adds a second and third landmark so the student must apply the rule to a whole set of times and use spacing as the comparison tool.
solution_step_plan: List the original key times $t=2$, $t=4$, and $t=6$.
Move each one by the same offset for $x(t-3)$ to get $t=5$, $t=7$, and $t=9$.
Solve $2t=2$, $2t=4$, and $2t=6$ for $x(2t)$ to get $t=1$, $t=2$, and $t=3$.
Compare the gaps: unchanged gaps indicate a shift, while halved gaps indicate compression.
practice_variation_axes: number of landmarks
whether the landmarks are equally spaced
shift amount
scale factor

sections.handoff_notes: Use the multiple key times to make the spacing rule explicit. The follow-up questions should mirror the worked example with new landmark values.

sections.section_title: Identifying Translation vs Compression from Key-Time Spacing
sections.learning_goal: Use the spacing between key times to decide whether a transformed signal is a translation or a compression or expansion.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the classification is based on symbolic spacing comparisons.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate an image. The step should classify transformation type from key-time spacing only.

question_policy.answer_format: Five text answer choices; each choice classifies the transformation and states the matching offset or factor.
question_policy.practice_question_model: A reference signal has key times at $t=1$ and $t=5$. Which transformed signal is a translation, which is a compression, and what factor or offset matches each one?
distractor_plan: Confuse preserved spacing with compression.
Treat the spacing ratio as a shift amount.
Use the wrong direction for the offset.
Mix up compression with expansion.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: N/A for the example step.
tutorial_outline.base_case: N/A for the example step.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: The signal $x(t)$ has key times at $t=1$ and $t=5$. One candidate transformed signal has them at $t=4$ and $t=8$; another has them at $t=1/2$ and $t=5/2$. Decide which candidate is a translation and which is a compression, and name the shift or scale factor.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that equal spacing from the reference signal identifies a translation, while uniformly reduced spacing identifies a compression with factor $2$.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Shifts the task from direct mapping to inference: the student must read the pattern in the spacings and decide which transformation produced it.
solution_step_plan: Measure the original spacing between the two key times.
Check whether each candidate preserves that spacing or multiplies it by a constant ratio.
If the spacing is unchanged, identify the translation offset; if it changes uniformly, identify the compression factor.
State the classification for both candidates in one sentence.
practice_variation_axes: spacing preserved or changed
compression factor
translation offset
number of key times used

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the classification step explicit. The questions should force the learner to infer shift versus scale from spacing rather than from direct substitution.

sections.section_title: Distinguishing Shift and Scale in Piecewise Signals
sections.learning_goal: Track piecewise breakpoints through a shift and a scale and use them to choose the correct transformed piecewise signal.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the piecewise signal is described by symbolic breakpoints.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate an image. Use text-only breakpoint lists and interval descriptions.

question_policy.answer_format: Five text answer choices; each choice gives transformed breakpoint locations or the correct transformation classification.
question_policy.practice_question_model: A piecewise signal has breakpoints at $t=a$ and $t=b$. Which answer choice correctly lists the transformed breakpoints in $x(t-c)$ and $x(dt)$?
distractor_plan: Shift only one breakpoint.
Multiply breakpoints instead of dividing for the scaled case.
Keep the original interval width after scaling.
Apply the shift with the wrong sign.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: N/A for the example step.
tutorial_outline.base_case: N/A for the example step.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: The piecewise signal $x(t)$ equals $2$ from $t=1$ to $t=4$ and $0$ elsewhere. Compare the breakpoints in $y_1(t)=x(t-2)$ and $y_2(t)=x(2t)$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that the breakpoints of the piecewise signal move by a constant offset under a shift and by division under a scale, while the signal levels stay the same.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Applies the comparison rule to breakpoint data instead of isolated landmark times, so the student must transform interval boundaries consistently.
solution_step_plan: Identify the original breakpoints at $t=1$ and $t=4$.
